paper_title: CANTraj: Recovering Vehicle Trajectories from CAN Signals in Naturalistic Driving

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Open driving releases and usage-based insurance programs often claim to prevent privacy breaches by omitting GPS records when sharing or collecting vehicle data. However, removing GPS coordinates from driving logs does not erase the location information carried by vehicle signals. While prior route-inference attacks have demonstrated that speed, steering, and driving events can be matched to road networks to reconstruct trajectories, existing studies rely on inconsistent prior assumptions and evaluation metrics and are tested only on small, restricted datasets, making their results difficult to compare and their real-world effectiveness uncertain. We release CANTraj, a naturalistic driving dataset pairing decoded CAN events with time-aligned GNSS trajectories (3,940 drives, 454 drivers), and CANTraj-Bench for evaluating trajectory recovery (3,675 drives, 431 drivers, 1,380 hours, 85,919 km). On 776 evaluation drives from 94 unseen drivers, we compare six re-implemented attacks and benchmark baselines under explicit information-access protocols, paired comparisons, and metrics incorporating failures. Experiments show that combining steering signals with road-network constraints yields the largest gain: With a known start and heading, adding steering to speed raises the online map filter's five-minute route recovery from 56% to 87%, with a median average displacement error of 43 m versus 921 m for map-free dead reckoning. Offline beam search recovers 88% of test routes with the heading and 81% without it. Because methods fail on different windows, we also evaluate an LLM harness that selects among candidate routes on 659 five-minute windows; its best configuration recovers 79% of routes on test and 83% on few-shot, outperforming the best baseline on test and matching it on few-shot. Data and code at huggingface.co/datasets/HenryYHW/CANTraj and github.com/WangYuHang-cmd/GPS--CAN.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: CANTraj: Recovering Vehicle Trajectories from CAN Signals in Naturalistic Driving Yuhang Wang1, Jingxin Yang2, Chuheng Wei3, Suyang Chen4, Haozhuang Chi5 and Hao Zhou1, 1University of South Florida, USA 2Stanford University, USA 3Purdue University, USA 4University of Florida, USA 5Nanyang Technological University, Singapore yuhangw@usf.edu, jingxiny@stanford.edu, wch@purdue.edu, suyang.chen@ufl.edu, chi0001@e.ntu.edu.sg, haozhou1@usf.edu AbstractOpen driving releases and usage-based insurance programs often claim to prevent privacy breaches by omitting GPS records when sharing or collecting vehicle data. However, removing GPS coordinates from driving logs does not erase the location information carried by vehicle signals. While prior routeinference attacks have demonstrated that speed, steering, and driving events can be matched to road networks to reconstruct trajectories, existing studies rely on inconsistent prior assumptions and evaluation metrics and are tested only on small, restricted datasets, making their results difficult to compare and their realworld effectiveness uncertain. We release CANTraj, naturalistic driving dataset pairing decoded CAN events with time-aligned GNSS trajectories (3,940 drives, 454 drivers), and CANTraj-Bench for evaluating trajectory recovery (3,675 drives, 431 drivers, 1,380 hours, 85,919 km). On 776 evaluation drives from 94 unseen drivers, we compare six re-implemented attacks and benchmark baselines under explicit information-access protocols, paired comparisons, and metrics incorporating failures. Experiments show that combining steering signals with road-network constraints yields the largest gain: With known start and heading, adding steering to speed raises the online map filters five-minute route recovery from 56 % to 87 %, with median average displacement error of 43 versus 921 for map-free dead reckoning. Offline beam search recovers 88 % of test routes with the heading and 81 % without it. Because methods fail on different windows, we also evaluate an LLM harness that selects among candidate routes on 659 five-minute windows; its best configuration recovers 79 % of routes on test and 83 % on few-shot, outperforming the best baseline on test and matching it on few-shot. Data and code are available at Hugging Face and GitHub. I. INTRODUCTION Modern cars broadcast wheel speed, steering angle, pedal positions and yaw rate over the controller area network (CAN) bus, which can be accessed through the on-board diagnostics (OBD) port. Usage-based insurance, fleet telematics, aftermarket driver assistance and public driving datasets collect these signals, as do studies of production driver-assistance systems [1], [2]. Removing global navigation satellite system (GNSS) coordinates may appear to protect location privacy, but the remaining vehicle signals can still reveal where car travelled [3], [4]. Existing attacks exploit speed patterns, driving events or steering geometry. Speed-based methods match stops, travelled distances and feasible turns to road network, using path search, hidden Markov models or particle filters [3], [4], [5], Corresponding author: Hao Zhou (haozhou1@usf.edu). [6]. Event-based methods derive routes from distances and turn directions [7], learn manoeuvres from brake signals (BBLT) [8], [9], or match events detected from speed and accelerator pedal position to road intersections (CAN-Trace) [10]. Steering-based attacks either match the steering profile to road curvature (SPy) [11] or combine vehicle motion model with map matching (MacroTracking and OPD-II) [12], [13]. Their outputs range from ranked destinations and candidate routes to position estimates along trip. These studies establish privacy risk, but their results remain difficult to compare across signals and methods. Their datasets differ in coverage and signal source: SPy evaluates 58 trips from five vehicle models, OPD-II reports 59 tracks from four cars, and Elastic Pathing uses 945 traces from two regions, including GPS-derived speeds [4], [11], [13], [14]. Comparing these published scores mixes differences in signals, algorithms, drivers, vehicles and road networks. The assumed knowledge also varies: known start and heading, containing area, or additional traffic information [10], [11], [13], [15]. Reported success can mean highly ranked destination, trajectory overlap, or nodes covered by the union of several candidate routes [3], [10], [13]; these scores do not measure the same recovery task. Individual sensitivity studies leave open how methods compare on the same drives, how much each signal adds with the reconstruction model fixed, and how accuracy, failures and cost change with the available information and trip duration. Data owners need these comparisons to assess CAN release; localisation systems need them when GNSS is unavailable. We address these gaps through CANTraj and CANTrajBench, with three research questions. RQ1: How accurately can existing methods recover trajectories, and which CAN signals improve recovery? RQ2: How do initial heading, online or offline access, and trip duration affect accuracy? RQ3: What explains failures, and how do accuracy, computational cost and resistance to degraded signals trade off? Our contributions are threefold. (I) Dataset and benchmark. We introduce CANTraj, naturalistic driving dataset of 3,940 drives from 454 drivers with decoded CAN signals and time-aligned GNSS trajectories. CANTraj-Bench uses 3,675 of these drives, spanning 1,380 hours and 85,919 km, to evaluate online and offline trajectory recovery from different combinations of CAN signals. It defines 97,340 evaluation episodes and specifies signal sources, map access, and failure scoring rule (Sections III and IV). (II) Unified cross-method comparison. We re-implement six published attacks and compare them with dead reckoning, map-based particle filtering, and offline beam search. Where available, we use the original authors sample data to check our implementations. The main evaluation covers 776 drives from 94 drivers across the test and few-shot splits, with paired comparisons on common episodes. We document each methods adaptations and information requirements (Section V) and separately evaluate an LLM harness that selects among candidate routes. (III) Recovery and failure analysis. Steering provides the largest gain among the CAN signals tested. With speed and steering, the median error on five-minute test windows is 43 for online map filtering and 921 for map-free dead reckoning. Offline beam search is less sensitive to missing initial heading than online filtering and avoids some of its largest errors on longer windows. Different methods recover different windows, and quantising steering to 10 or speed to 1 m/s leaves the tested map-based attacks largely effective (Section VI). II. RELATED WORK a) Route inference from vehicle signals: Early speedbased attacks search for destinations or paths consistent with stops, distances and feasible turns [3], [4], [14]. Wahlstrom et al. [6] use map particle filter with lateral-force and speedlimit constraints. Zhou et al. [5], [15] combine hidden Markov search and speed-sequence matching with traffic information. These studies include GPS-derived speed traces as well as OBD measurements, and the later Elastic Pathing and Zhou papers reuse earlier datasets. Their results demonstrate leakage from speed, but do not isolate the effect of signal source or decoder on common vehicle population. Richer signals expose additional route structure. BBLT and its journal extension infer manoeuvres from brake signals before searching the road network [8], [9]; CAN-Trace uses speed and pedal events [10]. Waltereit et al. [7] match distance and turn sequences, which can come from CAN or phone sensors, but evaluate GPS-derived events with injected errors. SPy matches steering to road curvature [11]; MacroTracking and OPD-II integrate speed and steering and correct the resulting path with map [12], [13]. Their evaluations answer different questions: MacroTracking measures proximity to reference path, OPD-II reports trajectory similarity, and CAN-Trace includes coverage by multiple candidates. We retain route and position metrics separately and count unsuccessful searches, so unsuccessful searches remain visible in the comparison. Vehicle localisation and learned motion models Map matching traditionally assigns noisy positions to roads [16], while sparse trajectory recovery also receives intermittent GPS positions [17]. Arc-length map matching uses vehicle sensors with known lane centreline and recent GPS initialisation [18]. These inputs differ from CAN release with only one known position. Learned navigation offers complementary designs: AI-IMU adapts filters measurement noise [19]; FormerReckoning and RoTrax learn from inertial sequences [20], [21]; S-TRAVERSE combines vehicle speed with smartphone IMU [22]. GHNet estimates heading from GNSS velocity [23], and rapid alignment methods use GNSS trajectory window [24], [25]. They motivate learned motion and heading studies, but their additional sensors or GNSS observations must be distinguished from CAN-only inputs. Our signal source labels make this distinction explicit. Location protection and evaluation data RAoPT and VehiTrack reconstruct trajectories from perturbed locations [26], [27]. TransProtect generates plausible substitute locations, while Olympus and adversarial mobility prediction learn representations that balance an authorised task with sensitive inference [27], [28], [29]. These studies motivate testing adaptive attacks and assessing downstream utility. In our experiments, map-based attacks using their original settings still recover routes from quantised CAN signals. Likewise, accuracy and computational cost should be reported together, as emphasised in trajectory-similarity evaluation [30]. Public driving datasets serve different purposes: comma2k19 provides CAN and GNSS for highway commute [31], while DriveDNA provides naturalistic data without GPS coordinates [32]. CANTraj adds paired CAN and GNSS data across hundreds of drivers and vehicle platforms, together with common evaluation of six attacks and controlled signal comparisons. III. TRAJECTORY RECOVERY TASK AND EVALUATION a) Task: We study how accurately vehicle can be tracked from CAN signals over different time windows when its starting position is known. Given the position p0 at time t0, each method uses the available vehicle signals to estimate the trajectory over [t0, t0 +D]. We query the method at the timestamps of recorded GPS fixes, with at most one fix per second and no interpolation. The method must return position estimate at each query time. If method outputs only route, we integrate the speed used by that method to obtain the distance travelled at each query time, then use that distance to locate the vehicle along the predicted route. For SPy [11], we use the time alignment from its own warping path. In this conversion, the GPS reference provides only the query timestamps. b) Priors and protocols: Three priors are switched independently, giving eight protocols written O/F-N/M-H+/H. Online (O): an event becomes visible only after its logged time, the episode length is unknown, and the method is queried as the reference seconds arrive; offline (F): all events of the episode are visible, nothing outside it. Map (M): an OpenStreetMap (OSM) drive network; the usable region is the disc of radius 5 km + 40 m/s (at most 60 km) around p0, and only that disc is visible to the benchmarks map methods (Section IV); OPD-IIs Meili matcher searches its Valhalla region tiles within 200 of the dead-reckoned trace and is not cut to the disc (Table I). Heading (H+): the GPS course at t0 is given; under it is withheld. The start position is always given, except to the two area adaptations, which receive 5 km square centred on it (Section V; the method does not read p0, but the squares placement uses it). This study reports five of the eight protocols: without the map only O-N-H+, with the map all four. Published methods are run under the protocol that matches their own assumptions and labelled with their look-ahead (OPD-II decides position up to 3 later). c) Inputs: Each method receives only the columns allowed by its signal set, and static vehicle parameters (wheelbase, steering ratio) come from the drives own logged car parameters unless variant is named calibrated (training-split calibration). Every signal is labelled by its source: C0 read from the vehicle bus (speed, steering angle, pedals, yaw rate), C1 derived from CAN inside the vehicle software, I0 the loggers raw inertial measurement unit (IMU), and produced by the driving softwares localizer, which used GPS in the software versions of this data. Class results are reported only as reference and never as CAN-only. Beyond the permitted start position and initial heading, GPS positions, speed, course, accuracy fields and absolute time are excluded. d) Episodes: An anchor t0 is GPS fix with speed 3 m/s, course accuracy 5 (and horizontal accuracy < 10 for the u-blox receiver) and CAN speed 2.5 m/s; p0 is the fixs position. Windows of 1, 5 and 15 minutes and the rest of the drive are cut from anchors; an episode is eligible when at least 80 % of its seconds have fix, no reference gap exceeds 30 and the path is at least 100 long. Windows of different lengths overlap and come from different drives, so the horizon study (RQ2) uses fixed cohort with one start per drive. e) Metrics: For an episode with errors et between prediction and reference: average displacement error (ADE, mean of et); coverage cr (share of seconds with et r, = 100 unless stated); time-free path recall and precision at 50 (share of the reference path within 50 of the predicted path and vice versa, both resampled at 5 m); route recovered = path recall@50 0.8, which says the route was followed, not that every second was right; the end-of-window error (reported as the share beyond 500 m). Two failure definitions are named separately: tail-lost (the final fifth of the window stays beyond 100 m) and terminal excursion (the window ends beyond 100 m; its onset is the first second after the last return within 100 m). The text reports ADE, c100, route recovered and the two failure shares; the released tables carry every metric. f) Failures and statistics: The episodes method is expected to answer are fixed before looking at its outputs (eligible episodes of the window, start on the map for map protocols, the methods signals valid on the drive, start heading if the method needs one). An expected episode without output (time-out, no match, error) is failure: its ADE is + in medians and distributions and its coverage and route flags are zero; means are reported only on episodes where every compared method has an output, next to the failure rate. Confidence intervals (CIs) are percentile bootstraps that resample drivers (one driver can own hundreds of drives; 1,000 resamples, 500 for the cohort and signal studies and 300 for the top-K analysis); driver-equal median summarises each driver first. Comparisons between methods or signal sets are paired on common episodes: paired median and mean differences use the episodes where both have an output, and the share of episodes where one method is closer counts its failures as losses (episodes where both fail are left out). paired interval that includes zero means that this sample gives no clear evidence either way, not that the two are equivalent. Five comparisons are primary: the map filter against the beam (steering, heading known), speed against speed and steering (signal study), heading known against unknown (beam and filter), OPD-II against the filter, and learned against nominal motion sources; every other comparison is exploratory, and its interval describes uncertainty without correction for multiplicity. For learned methods every statistic, bootstrap bounds included, is the mean over three training seeds, with the SD over seeds. IV. DATA AND QUALITY Fig. 1. Geographic distribution of the CANTraj drives. Gray gives the number of drives per country, and per state or province in the US panel. Track colour gives the continent. Tags give each regions drive count. One area is not drawn, and its drives are not counted in the gray levels. a) Corpus: CANTraj follows the collection and processing similar to DriveDNA [32]: naturalistic drives logged by aftermarket driver-assistance systems on the drivers own cars, with the raw logs re-decoded, cleaned and pseudonymised; unlike that release, which carries no GPS coordinates, it pairs CAN and GNSS. CANTraj-Bench uses 3,675 drives of 431 drivers, 266 vehicle platforms of 27 brands, 1,380 hours and 85,919 km: every raw log re-decoded into timestamped message tables (100 Hz where the full log was kept, 10 Hz for drives with only the compressed log); the drives GNSS track on the same time axis, with the first and last two minutes of every drive cut; quality metadata and the splits below (pseudonymous drivers, no absolute time, no raw identifiers, Fig 1). The release holds 3,940 drives of 454 drivers (1,659 hours of GNSS track): the drives above and 265 drives that passed the same GNSS checks but yield no eligible episode (Section III): 131 without an admissible anchor, 69 whose windows all have GNSS coverage below 80 %, and 65 whose vehicle platform is unconfirmed; they stay in the release for other windowing rules and are not used here. The drives map discs touch OpenStreetMap extract regions in 44 US states, 5 Canadian provinces and 35 further regions in Europe, Asia, Oceania and South America; North America dominates. Drivers are split into disjoint folds (train, validation, test, few-shot evaluation; 122 drives of 86 drivers belong to no fold and are not used); all reported results are on test (43 drivers, 302 drives) and few-shot (51 drivers, 474 drives), whose drivers never occur in training. b) GNSS Reference: The reference is the GNSS track logged with each drive, one real fix per second: modem receiver on 2,793 drives (about 1 Hz) and u-blox receiver on 882 drives (up to 10 Hz, reduced to 1 Hz). GNSS time lags the bus by receiver-dependent delay, estimated on the training fold by cross-correlating GNSS and CAN speed (0.7 modem, 0.2 u-blox) and applied to the reference for every method alike. Eligibility (Section III) leaves 1,917 test and 1,963 few-shot 5minute episodes, 608 and 565 15-minute episodes, and 282 and 460 whole-drive episodes. Drives whose vehicle platform could not be confirmed from the logged fingerprint are excluded from the CAN-only board (65 drives of 32 drivers). c) Signals: Speed and steering angle are present on almost every drive. The accelerator pedal position is continuous signal on only part of the brands (48 of 302 test and 64 of 474 few-shot drives); where present it correlates with the longitudinal acceleration, at brand-specific scale. The brake field mixes pedal position, pressure and torque across brands; the pedal-pressed flags are available almost everywhere. Methods that need the accelerator (CAN-Trace) or continuous pedals (the signal sets S2c and S4c of Section V) are therefore evaluated on the pedal-valid subset, and the pressed flags are separately named set (S2b, S4b), not substitute. d) Maps: Road graphs are cut from Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extracts of one snapshot into 0.25 tiles (drivable highway classes, one-way and turn restrictions). An audit of the first map build against its sources found 149 of the 5,111 needed tiles cut incompletely at the margins of early tiling passes (starts there had no road nearby, and map methods fell back to an arbitrary edge); every tile was re-cut from all intersecting extracts (the rebuilt road network), used by every map-based number here. With the rebuilt road network the median distance from the start to the nearest drivable road is 2.6 m; the 31 main-fold episodes without any road within 400 are excluded from the map protocols for all methods, by rule that looks at the map and the start only. Within one drive single cached graph serves all episodes, but each episode sees only the tiles of its own disc, with edge bearings in its local frame; exposing the whole per-drive graph changes no output (651 test windows of 60 drives: 100 % identical within 1 m; changed filter seed moves 19 %). V. METHODS AND SETUP Table lists every method with its signals, priors, look-ahead and use of training data; Fig. 2 shows the pipeline on one window. All methods share one replay engine: online methods receive the messages up to the query time, offline methods the whole episode, and the reference loader is disabled while any method runs. the released code, not a) Published methods: We re-implemented six published attacks under the benchmarks interface. Among these six attacks, we obtained OPD-II evaluation logs and MacroTracking sample trace; we use them to check our transcription against to recompute the papers scores. MacroTracking [12] (speed, steering; online): 1 deadreckoning updates and, every 20 m, pull toward the nearest road edge weighted by the distance to the next intersection. The released code works in Web Mercator units with the speed scaled by 1.1 (constants fitted to the authors car and city); we use metres and the logged speed. With the authors constants on their sample trace, the re-implementation stays within median of 7.1 of their committed trajectory. OPDII [13] (speed, steering): bicycle-model dead reckoning in 0.1 windows, re-snapped every 30 windows by Valhalla/Meili map matching [16] on the same road network; its released tool outputs each position once matched (at most 3 later), and we also report strictly online read-out. On 8 of the authors 59 sample logs, the re-implementation and the unmodified released script, run on the same decoded inputs and tiles, differ by median of at most 0.33 m. The authors per-car wheelbase values (3.85 to 4.9 m) and angle scaling are carspecific calibration of the bicycle model; we use the physical model with each drives own wheelbase and steering ratio (a training-calibrated variant changes the paired median by 0.1 m) and follow the code where it differs from the paper. Elastic Pathing [4], [14] (speed only; offline): best-first search over road paths that stretches or compresses the speed-integrated distance at stops and turns, with turn feasibility from road geometry and speed limits; we follow the 2017 version. Values the paper leaves open (side friction, the speed counted as stop) were chosen on validation drives only. CAN-Trace [10] (speed and accelerator pedal; offline): stops and pedal releases become nodes of line graph whose edge lengths come from integrated speed; the graph is matched to the intersection graph of the map by subgraph isomorphism with growing tolerance. Its original prior is an area containing the trip, not start point. We report known-start adaptation and an area adaptation whose road graph is cut to 5 km square centred on the known start: the method does not read p0, but the squares placement uses it, and window whose route leaves the square cannot be matched (Section VI-A). Its open values (the number of K-means clusters, the stop threshold of 0.05 m/s and the 1 % pedal-minimum band) were fixed without tuning. Dewri et al. [3] (speed only; offline): depth-first search from the known start keeps the road paths that pass an intersection at every stop of the trip, stay within 0.1 mile of shortest path, turn only where the speed is below 25 mph and end at the trip length; candidates are ranked by the likelihood of the observed speeds under speed-limit model that slows down at turns and stops. The paper ranks destinations; we lay the distance travelled along each of the top ten paths. No value was tuned; its search budget is Elastic Pathings, counted in node expansions and shared by the start edges. For the signal-combination study the same architecture gets second heading output, an unsigned turn magnitude, because without steering the direction of turn is not identifiable while its occurrence is; one decoder (the particle filter with perparticle turn budget for the magnitude not explained by the signed rate) is used for every signal set. The six signal sets are S1 (speed), S2c and S2b (S1 plus the continuous accelerator pedal or the pressed flags), S3 (speed and steering) and S4c and S4b (S3 plus the pedal or the flags); they differ only in which signal columns are non-zero and are trained on the same drives with the same budget. d) Setup: All runs use one workstation (Intel Core i912900K, 24 threads, 31 GB of memory; consumer GPU trains the learned models), Python 3.12 with NumPy, SciPy and PyTorch, and pyvalhalla 3.9.1 for OPD-II; the language model of Section VI-C2 is served from one H100 GPU on separate host. Search methods have per-episode budget (Elastic Pathing: 0.2 of search time per second of the window, 30 to 300 s, and 70 branch calls per second, 20,000 to 200,000; CAN-Trace: 120 and 200,000 expansions; Dewri et al. and SPy as stated above), and an episode whose search ends without result counts as failure. Parameters of the benchmark baselines were fixed in an earlier version on training and validation drives and not changed for this study. A. RQ1: Methods and signal contributions VI. RESULTS Table III summarises the findings. Table II and Fig. 3 show the main rows on the five-minute windows of the test drivers (1,917 windows, 42 drivers) and few-shot drivers (1,963 windows, 50 drivers; 1,959 under the map protocols after the map-start rule); all rows but the two area adaptations know the start position and, unless marked, the heading. Without map, every CAN-only method drifts far within five minutes. Nominal steering dead reckoning has median ADE of 921 on test and 1,669 on few-shot drivers, no better than straight line at the measured speed (735 m); training-fold calibration does not help on test (1,312 m). The learned GRU has the lowest no-map error (543 on test, 393 on fewshot drivers), clearly better than dead reckoning only on the few-shot drivers (on test the paired CI includes zero: 120 m, [592, 361]; Section VI-A1). sections.title: Evidence and scope
sections.content: RQ1 methods and signals RQ2 information and duration RQ3 failure and robustness The map and steering provide the largest gains; learned motion and pedals add little with the map. Five-minute test medians: steering DR 921 m, map filter 43 m. Signal comparisons fix the learner, decoder and drives. Offline decoding reduces sensitivity to initial heading and avoids some large tracking failures. Beam medians: 37 with heading, 41 without. Heading still changes route recovery from 81 to 88 %. Duration comparisons use the same drives. Methods fail on different windows; mild quantisation leaves the tested attacks effective. Per-window choice among ten methods: 98 % route recovery versus 88 % for the beam. Steering quantised to 10: at most 1.3 percentage points of change. among the steering map methods and says nothing about any vehicle or region. 1) Contribution of each signal: Does the model use an added signal at all? On validation chunks of 300 we shuffle one input block across chunks and recompute the fixed learners loss. Shuffling steering multiplies the loss by 3.4 to 3.8 (all seeds, with or without pedals); shuffling the continuous pedal changes it by 0.5 to +9.2 % next to speed alone and by +4.2 to +7.2 % next to speed and steering (three seeds each), the pressed flags by 2.4 to 1.2 % (one seed each): the pedals effect is small and, next to speed alone, not consistent across seeds. Steering provides the main signal gain. The controlled study uses 407 five-minute windows from 31 evaluation drivers with continuous accelerator signal. The learner, decoder and drives are fixed across signal sets, with three seeds for continuous inputs and one for pressed flags. Adding steering to speed changes the paired median error by 120 to 234 m; every seeds CI excludes zero, and the median falls from 339 to 49 m. Adding the continuous pedal changes it by 4.8 to 6.1 with speed alone (all CIs include zero) and by 6.4 to 0.9 with steering. Pressed flags slightly worsen the speed-only result (5.2 [0.8, 10.7]). This subset is harder for speed-based search than the full evaluation groups, so its gains should be interpreted within the paired study. The untrained map filter gives consistent result on all test windows: 43 with steering versus 286 with speed alone (paired difference 59.5 m). Without the heading, these become 138 and 1,773 m. Elastic Pathing is substantially better than the speed-only beam without the heading: paired difference 51.2 [212, 33.0]. Its speed-based turn constraints provide useful information that the baselines uniform junction choices omit. better motion model does not help with the map; without it, the gain is clear only on the few-shot drivers. Without the map the learned GRU and the learned physics residual lower the median error of nominal steering dead reckoning from 1,669 to 393 and 435 on few-shot drivers (paired 714 and 841 over three seeds, SD 115 and 75.8 m; CI excluding zero for 3 and 3 of 3 seeds; test CIs include zero). Used as the motion source of the same map filter, both are slightly worse than nominal steering (few-shot paired medians 5.4 and 11.3 m, CIs excluding zero for 2 and 3 of 3 seeds; on test 9.9 and 6.0 with CIs including zero). Even the localizers GPS-informed curvature, far more accurate without the map (84 against 921 m), gives the filter 44 m, no better than nominal steering: once the road network constrains the path, the heading rates accuracy matters little at five minutes. CAN yaw rate or gyroscope gives no reliable gain over steering. Without the map, the CAN yaw rate, which only some brands broadcast, differs from steering in opposite directions on the two folds (test, 658 windows of 11 drivers: 519 [2,305, 912]; fewshot, 188 of 12: 338 [1,184, 66.8]); with so few drivers this is inconclusive. The driver-assistance systems gyroscope (not CAN signal) is indistinguishable from steering on both folds (paired medians 28.1 and 38.9 on 667 test and 732 few-shot windows; both CIs include zero). B. RQ2: Initial heading, offline access and duration With steering, the start heading barely moves the offline beams median, unlike the filters; it still matters in the tail and, with speed alone, for the beam too. Without the start heading the online filters five-minute median grows from 43 to 138 on test (paired median difference 27.5 [41.4, 11.3]), while the offline beam moves only from 37 to 41 (paired median difference 0.0 m; knowing the heading makes it closer in only 16 % of the episodes). Where it helps, the gain is large: the paired mean difference is 395 [554, 206] (filter 599 m), and the share of routes recovered falls from 88 to 81 % (filter 87 to 79 %). With speed alone the offline beam depends strongly on the heading (165 against 1,314 m). The same holds on fifteen-minute windows (149 vs 155 m; paired means in the released tables). decoder that sees the whole window can test every start direction against the later turns; the online filter, plausibly, must spread its particles over them until the first turn tells them apart. With the heading known, offline access buys little at the median, about half of it through the output. On test windows the paired median difference between the offline beam and the online filter is 2.7 [3.0, 2.0]. The heaviest-lineage output of the same filter (same particles and motion model) differs from the filter by paired median of 1.4 [2.3, 0.9]; beam and lineage differ by 0.5 [1.3, 0.3] (CI includes zero) at the median and in the tail on fifteen-minute few-shot windows (paired mean 221 [464, 43.3]; test CI includes zero). Horizon on one cohort. The cohort is the first fifteen-minute window of each of 426 test and few-shot drives (81 drivers), cut at 1, 5 and 15 minutes from the same start  (Fig. 5)  . On the 205 test drives, OPD-II has the lowest median after one minute (11 m, unpaired; the map filter 19 m), but the median of the offline beam with steering grows least: 17, 44 and 303 at 1, 5 and 15 minutes, against 19, 56 and 672 for the online filter and 1,316 and 1,351 for OPD-II and MacroTracking at fifteen minutes (unpaired). Paired on the same windows, beam and filter agree on most of them (paired median difference at fifteen minutes 3.1 [6.1, 1.6]) and the beam avoids the filters largest failures (mean difference 552 [1,421, 98.6]); the lineage output behaves like the filter here (paired mean against the beam 547 [1,390, 109]), so the beams search, not its single-path output, avoids these failures. The speed-only methods are kilometres off after fifteen minutes (Elastic Pathing 3,335 m, 11 of the 205 drives without complete path; beam 5,352 m). This cohort is harder than the pooled fifteen-minute comparison (filter 178 there). Whole drives. Drive duration differs between the two evaluation groups (median 19 versus 11 minutes), so results are reported separately. In 18 of 282 test and 36 of 454 fewshot drives, the endpoint lies outside the 60 km map disc. Methods restricted to that disc cannot recover the tail. The steering beam has the lowest CAN-only median on both groups (1,179 and 94 m); removing the heading gives 1,244 and 124 m. The ranking of the filter, MacroTracking and OPD-II differs between groups and is descriptive: intervals overlap, these comparisons are unpaired, and Meilis map access differs. Speed-only searches are kilometres off, while SPy with start and heading recovers only 4 and 6 % of whole-drive routes. C. RQ3: Failures, cost and robustness Without steering, good candidate is often present but ranked low, and more often absent. The offline beam keeps ten complete paths (the best-of-K curves are in the released figure data). With speed alone and no start heading its topranked path has median error of 1,314 on test, the best of its top three 210 and the best of ten 72 m; the best path is ranked first in only 21 % of the windows. With steering the gap closes (41 at rank one, 27 for the best of ten, best path first in 54 %). Elastic Pathings stopping rule usually leaves single complete path (1,484 of its 1,855 test outputs), so its top-K adds little (129 to 96 m). Dewri et al.s ten candidates behave like the speed-only beams (293 to 49 m, best first in 39 %). Splitting the test windows by 50 whole-path criterion separates the two failure kinds: with speed alone and no start heading, the beams top-ranked path is within 50 of the reference in 18 % of the windows, lower-ranked candidate is while the top one is not in 24 % (a ranking failure), and no candidate is in 58 % (a search failure); with steering the shares are 61, 10 and 28 %. The top-K gains come from the ranking failures; most speed-only windows have no good candidate at all. The beams candidate score does not tell an attacker when it is right, unless speed is all it has. Each beam candidate carries score normalised over the surviving candidates (a confidence score, not calibrated probability): with one path or near-duplicates the score is 1 whatever the outcome (29 % of the test windows with steering). With steering the Top-1 score separates recovered from unrecovered routes no better than chance (AUROC 0.47, CI [0.41, 0.52] on test, 0.49 on few-shot drivers; Spearman correlation with the ADE 0.01): threshold of 0.9 accepts 46 % of the test windows at route rate of 87 %, and 13 % of the accepted routes are wrong. With speed alone the candidates differ and the score is informative (AUROC 0.81 with the heading, 0.65 without; threshold of 0.9 accepts 13 % of the windows at route rate of 97 % against 54 % overall). Elastic Pathing and Dewri et al. give score of 1 to 69 and 87 % of their outputs (one path, or uniformly scored paths), so no selection is possible there. With steering, the filters and the beams losses start disproportionately just after turns; the speed-only filters do not. fifteen-minute window is lost when it ends in terminal excursion (Section III). With steering, 73 % of the filters 1,169 fifteen-minute windows (test and few-shot pooled) and 70 % of the beams end lost, and the onsets cluster just after turns: 43 % and 38 % of them fall within 30 after reference turn, against about 23 and 22 % if onsets were spread evenly over the window; this is an association (most onsets fall elsewhere; folds pooled; the published methods and the speed-only beam were not analysed). The speed-only filter is lost in 93 % of the windows, with no such link to turns (23 against 22 %). The speed-only map filter has much larger errors in denser road networks; the steering methods differ less, and mainly over longer horizons. Split by road density around the start (tertiles at 56 and 246 nodes per km2; folds pooled; 1,292 windows of 33, 82 and 81 drivers per tertile, sparse to dense), the filter with steering has five-minute medians of 29, 39 and 36 from sparse to dense, while the speed-only filter goes from 73 to 677 and 843 m. The steering filter is not unaffected: its five-minute tail-lost share rises from 17 to 27 % and its fifteen-minute median (374 windows per tertile) from 89 to 264 (beam 77 to 162 m). Density is confounded with region, driver, speed and fold, so these are associations, not effects. The methods fail on different windows; almost no window defeats all of them, and the common failures sit in the windows with many turns. For each five-minute window we take the best of the ten map methods with the start heading, by the lowest ADE or by route recovery (two oracles). Some method recovers the route in 98 % of the test windows (fewshot 98 %) against 88 % for the beam, our fixed reference, difference of 10 points (CI [6, 16]); none of them recovers it in 2.3 % of the windows (CI [1.4, 3.6]). This common failure grows from 0.1 % of the windows with at most one reference turn to 8.7 % with seven or more (test and few-shot pooled, 402 windows) and from 0.9 to 2.9 % across the density tertiles. No method attains the per-window minimum ADE in more than 22 % of the windows (OPD-II; lineage 22, beam 19 %); Fig. 5. The same 205 test drives (37 drivers), one start each, scored 1, 5 and 15 minutes after the start: median ADE with driver-resampling 95 % bands. Online methods are scored on prefixes of their 15-minute runs; offline methods are rerun on each prefix with only its signals and map. Encoding as in Fig. 3. the oracle improves on the beams ADE by paired median of 3.4 [5.4, 2.3]. These are facts about the current method set, not about what is recoverable: methods that share motion model, map or search share failures too. Per driver (36 test drivers with at least five windows), the beams route share has median of 88 % and is below 50 % for 3 % of them. 1) Computational cost and degraded signals: Inference is usually inexpensive; map preparation is separate cost. Timing uses fixed validation subset of 92 windows, with one method and one worker at time; failed searches retain their elapsed time. For five-minute windows, median times are 0.03 for steering dead reckoning, 0.08 for MacroTracking, 0.08 for OPD-II, 0.24 for the beam and 0.57 for the filter. Elastic Pathing has long tail (90th percentile 0.13 s). SPys area search takes 4.93 at the median and exhausts its budget on 9 of 76 windows. CAN-Trace is timed separately on 25 pedal-valid windows: 0.63 with the start known and 0.09 with the area prior, usually without match. Building drives graph takes 2.6 at the median; peak memory is at most 2.1 GB. Preparing all road tiles takes 46 minutes, while Valhalla preparation takes 44 minutes and 3.4 GB on disk. Smaller particle and beam budgets lose little accuracy in the supplementary comparisons. Degraded signals barely change dead reckoning, and the fixed map attacks tolerate most coarsening. Quantising the speed to 1 m/s, adding 0.5 m/s of speed noise or sampling the steering at 1 Hz moves the paired median error of steering dead reckoning by at most 0.4 on either fold, against errors of hundreds of metres. For the map attacks we re-ran the steering filter and beam and the speed-only beam on the five-minute windows of both evaluation folds with one signal degraded before the method sees it, every parameter unchanged, on grid fixed before the first run (per-level curves in the released figure data): steering-wheel angle quantised to 2, 5, 10 or 20, held at 1 or 0.2 Hz or offset by per-second noise of 2 or 5 (one seed); speed quantised to 1, 2 or 5 m/s or held at

Drivers are separate across splits; vehicle platforms and regions are not. Road-density and turn-count comparisons are associations because road conditions, drivers and vehicles vary together. Method rankings change on the controlled supplement (Section VI-A), so they should not be treated as universal. Continuous pedal and CAN yaw signals are available on smaller subsets. The task mainly measures recovery after one position is known. The area variants receive square centred on that position and are not tests of unrestricted unknown-start tracking; many routes leave the square. OPD-IIs Meili map access also differs from the disc used by the other map methods. Checks against the authors samples support the implementation of MacroTracking and OPD-II, but do not reproduce every original experiment. The other four attacks lack the same validation evidence. Failure of these methods gives no privacy guarantee, and the per-window oracle is diagnostic result, not deployable selector. c) Reproducibility: CANTraj and CANTraj-Bench contribute paired CANGNSS data, common evaluation of trajectory recovery, and evidence on the roles of steering, maps, prior information and decoding. The results show substantial location leakage from vehicle signals and substantial variation across methods and driving conditions. Data, code and evaluation files are available at https: //huggingface.co/datasets/HenryYHW/CANTraj and https:// github.com/WangYuHang-cmd/GPS--CAN. comparison and scoring tools, twelve turns and forty calls; B+ runs and scores every preset. Full prompts and settings are in the supplement. On test drivers, route recovery is 69 % for the beam, 75 % for the selector and 75 % for the base agent (Table IV). The agent-minus-selector difference is 0.1 percentage points [1.6, 3.4] on test and 0.7 [2.6, 2.8] on few-shot drivers. Thus the base agent has no clear advantage over the selector, while its estimated serial cost is 36.4 per window versus 1.1 s. The extended agent reaches 78 % on test but 81 % on few-shot drivers; its combined recovery does not improve over the base agent (0.4 points [2.8, 2.0]). On test drivers, the extended agent improves over its selector by 4.1 points [1.3, 7.6], but the improvement does not extend to the few-shot group. An oracle choosing from the available candidates would recover 83 % of test routes with three tools and 87 % with all presets, indicating substantial room to improve selection. These results concern one model and two configurations. VII. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION a) Implications for reconstruction and data release: On these data, speed and steering with road map recover five-minute routes with errors of tens of metres. Offline beam search reduces large failures over longer windows and needs the initial heading less than online tracking does. For online use, the map filter and OPD-II have similar paired median errors at five minutes, while the filter recovers more routes and has fewer large errors. With speed alone, Elastic Pathing benefits from speed-based turn constraints that the benchmark filter and beam omit. These comparisons favour matching the method to the available signals and information, rather than choosing more complex motion model by default. For data publishers, removing GPS coordinates or initial heading does not remove route information. The continuous accelerator pedal adds little to speed and steering in our controlled comparison, but this does not establish that pedal or speed releases are safe.
